fatima-al-fihri#text: Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan in present-day Tunisia and moved with her family to Fez in Morocco, which was then flourishing under the Idrisids. After the death of her father, a wealthy merchant, she used her inheritance in 859 to found the al-Qarawiyyin mosque, named after the immigrants from Kairouan; her sister Maryam is said to have founded the Andalusian mosque at the same time. According to tradition, Fatima fasted throughout the construction. A place of teaching developed at the mosque for the Quran, law, grammar, mathematics and astronomy, where scholars such as Ibn Khaldun later studied or taught; the University of al-Qarawiyyin exists to this day and is often described as the oldest continuously operating institution of higher learning in the world.
ibn-ruschd#role: Philosopher, judge and physician in al-Andalus
ibn-ruschd#summary: The scholar from Córdoba whose commentaries on Aristotle shaped Christian and Jewish philosophy in the Middle Ages.
ibn-ruschd#text: Ibn Rushd came from a family of legal scholars in Córdoba and himself became chief judge in Seville and Córdoba as well as personal physician to the Almohad caliphs. Besides a medical handbook he wrote short, middle and long commentaries on the works of Aristotle, in which he freed the philosopher's teaching from later additions, and he defended philosophy as the duty of the thinking believer. In 1195 he was charged on account of these views and banished to Lucena, but was rehabilitated shortly before his death in Marrakesh in 1198. In Europe he was so influential under the name Averroes that the church banned the teachings of his followers in Paris in 1277; the Jewish philosopher Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas built on his writings.
rumi#summary: The mystic from Konya whose poems on the love of God are among the most widely read works of world literature.
rumi#text: Rumi was born in 1207 in Balkh in present-day Afghanistan; his family fled westward from the Mongols and settled around 1228 in Konya, the capital of the Seljuks of Rum, from which he took his name. There he worked as a legal scholar and preacher until his meeting with the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz in 1244 made him a poet and a mystic. His main work, the Masnavi with some 25,000 couplets, combines stories, Quranic interpretation and the teachings of Sufism; to this are added thousands of poems on the soul's longing for God. From the circle of his students arose the Mevlevi order, whose dervishes worship God with their whirling dance; his tomb in Konya remains a place of pilgrimage today.
timur#summary: The ruler of Samarkand who spread fear with campaigns from India to Anatolia while maintaining a brilliant court.
timur#text: Timur was born in 1336 near Kesh south of Samarkand into a Turco-Mongol tribe; an injury left him with a limp, from which the names Timur Lenk and Tamerlane arose. Since he was not descended from Genghis Khan, he formally ruled in the name of Mongol puppet khans, but saw himself as the restorer of the Mongol empire and a defender of Islam. From 1370 until his death he led campaigns into Persia, Russia, India, Syria and Anatolia that were of extraordinary cruelty toward cities that resisted. In Samarkand he had splendid buildings such as the Bibi-Khanym Mosque erected, and in 1401 he received the historian Ibn Khaldun outside Damascus for long conversations. His descendants, the Timurids, made Samarkand and Herat centers of astronomy, painting and poetry in the 15th century.
ibn-chaldun#role: Historian, statesman and founder of social science
ibn-chaldun#summary: The scholar from Tunis who in his Muqaddimah was the first to examine the laws governing the rise and fall of empires.
ibn-chaldun#text: Ibn Khaldun came from a family of scholars driven out of Seville and was born in Tunis in 1332. As secretary, envoy and minister he served changing rulers in North Africa and Granada, was imprisoned several times, and withdrew in 1375 to a castle in Algeria, where he wrote the Muqaddimah, the introduction to his world history. In it he explained the changing fortunes of empires through the cohesion of groups, asabiyyah: nomadic tribes with a strong sense of solidarity conquer softened cities, lose their own strength there within a few generations, and are replaced by new conquerors. From 1382 he lived in Cairo as a judge and professor at al-Azhar; in 1401 he negotiated with Timur outside besieged Damascus. His study of economy, climate, rule and society is regarded today as a forerunner of sociology and historical scholarship.
konrad-adenauer#role: First chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany
konrad-adenauer#summary: Bound the young Federal Republic firmly to the West and laid the ground for prosperity, sovereignty and reconciliation with France.
konrad-adenauer#text: Adenauer was mayor of Cologne from 1917 to 1933, was removed by the National Socialists and temporarily imprisoned. In 1949, at 73, he was elected the first federal chancellor by a majority of one vote and governed for 14 years. Against fierce resistance he pushed through integration with the West: accession to the Coal and Steel Community and in 1955 to NATO, rearmament, reparations to Israel, and in 1963 the Élysée Treaty with France; in 1955 he secured in Moscow the release of the last German prisoners of war. Critics accused him of sacrificing reunification to the freedom of the West and of tolerating former Nazis in the administration. Germans nevertheless reelected him three times; he stepped down in 1963.
nikita-chruschtschow#role: Soviet party leader and head of government
nikita-chruschtschow#summary: Denounced Stalin's crimes, sent Sputnik into space and faced Kennedy in the Cuban Missile Crisis.
nikita-chruschtschow#text: The son of a miner rose under Stalin to become party leader of Ukraine and of Moscow and prevailed in the power struggle after Stalin's death in 1953. In a secret speech at the party congress in 1956 he condemned Stalin's terror and cult of personality and released millions of prisoners, but in the same year had the Hungarian uprising crushed with tanks. His policy of peaceful coexistence alternated with threats: in 1958 he issued an ultimatum over Berlin, in 1961 he approved the building of the Wall, and in 1962 he stationed missiles in Cuba, which he withdrew after thirteen days. With Sputnik and Gagarin he won prestige for the Soviet Union, and trouble with failed agricultural reforms. In 1964 the Politburo removed him; he died a pensioner in Moscow.
martin-luther-king#role: Baptist minister and leader of the American civil rights movement
martin-luther-king#summary: Led the nonviolent struggle against racial segregation in the United States and gave the I Have a Dream speech in 1963.
martin-luther-king#text: King grew up in Atlanta in a family of ministers and became the voice of the Black civil rights movement through the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955. Following Gandhi's example he relied on marches, sit-ins and civil disobedience; arrests, bomb attacks on his house and FBI surveillance did not stop him. Before 250,000 people at the March on Washington in 1963 he invoked his dream of a country in which people are not judged by the color of their skin; in 1964, at the age of 35, he received the Nobel Peace Prize, and the civil rights and voting rights acts of 1964 and 1965 ended legal discrimination. In his last years he fought against poverty and the Vietnam War. On 4 April 1968 he was shot in Memphis.
rosa-parks#role: Civil rights activist in the United States
rosa-parks#summary: Her refusal to give up her seat on a bus to a white passenger set off the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955.
rosa-parks#text: Rosa Parks worked as a seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, and had been secretary of the local civil rights organization, the NAACP, since 1943, for which she documented cases of violence against Black people. On 1 December 1955 she refused to give up her seat to a white passenger, was arrested and fined; her steadfastness gave the signal for the boycott that brought down segregation on the buses. She lost her job, received death threats and moved to Detroit in 1957, where she worked for decades for a congressman and continued to campaign for civil rights. Congress honored her in 1999 with its highest award; after her death she was the first woman to lie in state in the Capitol.
ho-chi-minh#role: Founder and president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam
ho-chi-minh#summary: Led Vietnam in the struggle for independence against France and into the war against the United States.
ho-chi-minh#text: The son of a scholar left the French colony of Indochina in 1911 as a ship's cook, lived in London, Paris, Moscow and China, and in 1920 was among the founders of the French Communist Party. In 1941 he founded the independence movement Viet Minh, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi on 2 September 1945 and led the war against France, which ended in 1954 with the victory at Dien Bien Phu and the division of the country. As president of North Vietnam he supported the guerrilla struggle in the South and, in the war against the United States, rejected any compromise that gave up the unity of Vietnam. He died in 1969, six years before victory; the captured capital Saigon was named after him in 1976.
deng-xiaoping#role: Reform politician and de facto leader of the People's Republic of China
deng-xiaoping#summary: Opened China to the market economy from 1978 and made it a rising economic power, but had the democracy movement crushed in 1989.
deng-xiaoping#text: Deng encountered communism as a work-study student in France, took part in the Long March and rose to become one of Mao's closest associates. During the Cultural Revolution he was stripped of power twice and banished to work in a tractor factory. After Mao's death he prevailed in 1978 and began the policy of reform and opening: farmers were again allowed to produce for the market, special economic zones such as Shenzhen attracted foreign capital, students went abroad; with the saying that it did not matter whether a cat was black or white as long as it caught mice, he justified his pragmatism. In 1984 he agreed with Margaret Thatcher on the return of Hong Kong. He rejected political freedom and in June 1989 had the protests on Tiananmen Square ended with tanks. His course made China the second largest economy in the world within a single generation.
tim-berners-lee#role: British computer scientist and inventor of the World Wide Web
tim-berners-lee#summary: Developed the World Wide Web at CERN and waived patents so that it would be open to everyone.
tim-berners-lee#text: Berners-Lee, the son of two computer pioneers, studied physics at Oxford and worked as a software developer at the European research center CERN. To link the scattered documents of the physicists, he proposed a system of hyperlinks in 1989 and in 1990 wrote the first browser and the first web server, along with the foundations HTML, HTTP and URL. He ensured that CERN released the technology free of charge in 1993, and in 1994 founded the World Wide Web Consortium, which still sets open standards today. He was knighted for his invention in 2004 and honored with the Turing Award in 2016. For years he has warned about the power of the large platforms and campaigned for the protection of personal data and an open web.
angela-merkel#role: First female chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany
angela-merkel#summary: Led Germany from 2005 to 2021 through the financial, euro, refugee and coronavirus crises and shaped European politics.
angela-merkel#text: Angela Merkel grew up in East Germany as the daughter of a pastor, earned a doctorate in physics and entered politics only during the peaceful revolution of 1989. Under Helmut Kohl she became a minister, in 2000 leader of the CDU, and on 22 November 2005 the first woman to become chancellor. In sixteen years in office she saved banks and euro states with billions in aid during the financial and euro crises, decided after Fukushima in 2011 to phase out nuclear power, and in 2015 opened the borders to hundreds of thousands of refugees with the words we can do this, which brought her admiration and sharp criticism at home and abroad. During the coronavirus pandemic she explained the situation to citizens in televised addresses. Her policy toward Russia, above all the dependence on Russian gas, was sharply questioned after the attack on Ukraine in 2022.
justinian-i#summary: The Byzantine emperor who codified Roman law, built the Hagia Sophia and tried to reconquer the West.
justinian-i#text: Justinian came from a peasant family in the Balkans and succeeded his uncle Justin on the throne in 527. He saw himself as the restorer of the Roman Empire: his generals conquered the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy, his commission of jurists under Tribonian compiled all of Roman law in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, and his building program culminated in the Hagia Sophia. He survived the Nika riot of 532 only thanks to the resolve of his wife Theodora. His wars and an outbreak of plague from 541 exhausted the empire, which soon lost most of the conquests again.
theodora#summary: The actress who rose to become the most powerful woman in Byzantium and strengthened the rights of women.
theodora#text: Theodora was the daughter of a bear keeper in the circus of Constantinople and performed as an actress, a profession that at the time excluded women from society. Justinian had a law changed specifically so that he could marry her in 525, and he raised her to be co-ruler. When the Nika riot threatened the palace in 532 and the emperor wanted to flee, she declared, according to Procopius, that the purple made a fine shroud, and moved him to stay. She pushed through laws against forced prostitution and in favor of divorced women and protected the persecuted Miaphysites in the east of the empire. Her mosaic portrait in San Vitale in Ravenna is among the most famous works of art of the period.
otto-i#summary: The victor at the Lechfeld, whose imperial coronation in 962 marks the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire.
otto-i#text: Otto was crowned king at Aachen in 936 and prevailed in years of fighting against rebellious dukes and his own relatives. He bound the bishops and imperial abbeys closely to the crown, endowed them with land and sovereign rights and made them the support of his rule. After the victory over the Hungarians in 955 and the founding of the archbishopric of Magdeburg as a base for missions to the Slavs, he marched to Italy and received the imperial crown in 962. His second wife Adelaide and his brother Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, were important co-rulers; his tomb lies in Magdeburg Cathedral.
thomas-von-aquin#summary: The Dominican who sought to unite faith and reason in his Summa Theologica and brought scholasticism to its height.
thomas-von-aquin#text: Thomas came from a noble family near Aquino in southern Italy and entered the mendicant order of the Dominicans against the will of his family. He studied under Albertus Magnus in Cologne and Paris, where he later taught himself, and in only two decades produced an enormous body of work, including commentaries on Aristotle and the unfinished Summa Theologica. Unlike many of his contemporaries he held the philosophy of Aristotle, which had reached Europe through Averroes and Avicenna, to be compatible with Christian faith, since for him reason and revelation came from the same source. He died in 1274 on the way to the Council of Lyon; in 1323 he was canonized and his teaching became the foundation of Catholic theology.
eleonore-von-aquitanien#role: Duchess of Aquitaine, queen of France and England
eleonore-von-aquitanien#summary: The most powerful woman of the 12th century, who married two kings, accompanied a crusade and fostered courtly culture.
eleonore-von-aquitanien#text: As heiress to the vast duchy of Aquitaine, Eleanor married the French king Louis VII in 1137 and accompanied him on the Second Crusade in 1147. After that marriage was annulled in 1152 she married Henry Plantagenet, who two years later became King Henry II of England; their combined holdings reached from Scotland to the Pyrenees. At her court in Poitiers the poetry of the troubadours flourished. Because she supported her sons in a revolt against their father, Henry kept her in confinement for fifteen years; after his death she governed for her son Richard the Lionheart and raised the ransom for his captivity. She died at a great age in the abbey of Fontevraud.
friedrich-ii-staufer#role: Holy Roman emperor and king of Sicily
friedrich-ii-staufer#summary: The learned Hohenstaufen emperor whom contemporaries called the wonder of the world and who regained Jerusalem without a blow of the sword.
friedrich-ii-staufer#text: Frederick grew up an orphan in Sicily, where Arab, Greek, Jewish and Latin cultures met, and spoke several languages. Crowned emperor in 1220, he built Sicily into a tightly administered state with the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231 and founded the University of Naples in 1224. On his crusade in 1228 he won Jerusalem through a treaty with the sultan al-Kamil, even though the pope had excommunicated him. He wrote a treatise on falconry based on his own observation and supported poets and scholars. His decades-long struggle with the popes ended only with his death in 1250, and a few years later the Hohenstaufen line died out.
pachacutec#summary: The ninth Inca, who turned the city-state of Cusco into an empire and shaped its administration, roads and buildings.
pachacutec#text: Only oral traditions, recorded by Spanish chroniclers in the 16th century, tell of Pachacuti. According to them he saved Cusco from the Chanka as a young prince, stripped his father Viracocha of power and ruled from about 1438 to 1471. He organized the conquered land into provinces, resettled population groups, introduced the sun cult as the imperial religion and had Cusco laid out anew in the shape of a puma with the sun temple Coricancha. Terraces, canals and roads supplied the growing population, and the royal estate of Machu Picchu is attributed to him. His son Tupac Yupanqui continued the conquests.
michelangelo#summary: The creator of the David, the Sistine ceiling and the dome of St. Peter's, who embodies the High Renaissance like no other.
michelangelo#text: Michelangelo grew up in Florence and as a youth was supported in the household of Lorenzo de' Medici. With the Pietà in St. Peter's and the David he became famous before he was thirty; between 1508 and 1512 he painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel with more than 300 figures for Pope Julius II, although he regarded himself above all as a sculptor. Later he created the Last Judgment on the altar wall, planned the Medici Chapel and from 1547 directed the building of St. Peter's, whose dome he designed. He worked until shortly before his death at almost 89.
erasmus-von-rotterdam#summary: The most famous scholar of his time, who wanted to reform the church with satire and learning but rejected schism.
erasmus-von-rotterdam#text: Born the illegitimate child of a priest, Erasmus entered a monastery but left it and lived as an independent scholar in Paris, England, Italy and Basel. His Praise of Folly of 1511 mocked monks, theologians and popes, and his Greek New Testament of 1516 laid the groundwork for the Bible translations of the Reformation. Although many saw him as a forerunner of Luther, he broke with him in 1524 in his treatise on free will, because he abhorred conflict and violence. To this day he is regarded as a pioneer of tolerance and of European learning.
johannes-calvin#summary: The French reformer whose strict teaching and church order shaped Protestantism in Western Europe and North America.
johannes-calvin#text: Calvin studied law and theology in France, had to flee as a supporter of the Reformation and published the Institutes, the systematic statement of his teaching, in Basel in 1536. From 1541 he shaped Geneva into a city where church and council jointly watched over faith and conduct; services, schools and moral discipline were strictly regulated, and his opponent Michael Servetus was burned as a heretic in 1553. At the core of his theology was the doctrine of predestination, according to which God has destined people for salvation or damnation. Huguenots, Dutch, Scots and Puritans carried his teaching into the world.
ignatius-von-loyola#summary: The Basque nobleman and soldier who became the founder of an order after a wound and led the Catholic renewal.
ignatius-von-loyola#text: While defending Pamplona in 1521, a cannonball shattered Ignatius's leg; during his recovery he read legends of the saints and resolved to devote his life to God. He studied in Paris, where in 1534 he took a vow with six companions, and in 1540 received confirmation of the Society of Jesus from Pope Paul III. The Jesuits committed themselves to strict obedience to the pope, founded outstanding schools and universities and carried out missions from Brazil to Japan and China. His Spiritual Exercises, a guide to prayer and self-examination, are still practiced today.
sueleyman-der-praechtige#summary: The sultan under whom the Ottoman Empire reached its greatest power and advanced to the gates of Vienna.
sueleyman-der-praechtige#text: Suleiman ruled from 1520 to 1566 and conquered Belgrade, Rhodes, large parts of Hungary after the Battle of Mohács in 1526, and Baghdad; in 1529 he besieged Vienna in vain. His fleets dominated the eastern Mediterranean, and his alliance with France against Charles V made him a player in European politics. In his own empire he was called the Lawgiver, because he reorganized administration, taxation and law; his architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul. His wife Hürrem, a former slave, gained great political influence.
akbar#summary: The most significant ruler of the Mughal Empire, who united India and created a religiously tolerant court.
akbar#text: Akbar, a grandson of Babur, came to the throne in 1556 at the age of thirteen and ruled for almost fifty years. Although he himself never learned to read, he had books read aloud to him, assembled a library of thousands of manuscripts and fostered painting, music and architecture. In his House of Worship he debated with scholars of all religions and tried to bridge their differences with a court religion of his own. In the end his empire covered most of the Indian subcontinent and was richer than any state in Europe.
isabella-von-kastilien#summary: The queen who united Spain with her husband Ferdinand, conquered Granada and financed the voyage of Columbus.
isabella-von-kastilien#text: Isabella prevailed as queen of Castile in a war of succession in 1474 and ruled jointly with her husband Ferdinand of Aragon, with whom she joined the two largest kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula. In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs completed the Reconquista with the conquest of Granada, expelled the Jews from Spain in the same year and relied on the Inquisition founded in 1478. Also in 1492, Isabella gave Columbus the means for his voyage west and thereby secured Spain's access to the Americas. She ordered that the indigenous population must not be enslaved, though in practice this had little effect.
thomas-jefferson#role: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president of the United States
thomas-jefferson#summary: The plantation owner and Enlightenment thinker from Virginia who formulated the ideals of the American Revolution while holding slaves.
thomas-jefferson#text: Jefferson, a lawyer and landowner from Virginia, wrote the draft of the Declaration of Independence in 1776 at the age of 33, with the statement that all men are created equal. As envoy in Paris he witnessed the beginning of the French Revolution in 1789 and advised Lafayette on the Declaration of the Rights of Man; as the first secretary of state and from 1801 as president, he stood for the rights of the individual states and an America of free farmers. In 1803 he bought the Louisiana Territory from France and thereby doubled the area of the United States. A broadly educated architect, inventor and founder of the University of Virginia, he owned slaves all his life, among them Sally Hemings, with whom he had several children; this contradiction with his ideals shapes his image to this day. He died on 4 July 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration of Independence.
marie-antoinette#summary: The daughter of Maria Theresa who as queen became the target of hatred toward the court and died under the guillotine in 1793.
marie-antoinette#text: The Austrian archduchess was married at 14 to the heir to the French throne in order to strengthen the alliance between Habsburg and Bourbon, and became queen in 1774. Her spending on clothes, festivities and the Trianon estate, the affair of the diamond necklace in 1785 in which she was entangled through no fault of her own, and pamphlets mocking her as a wasteful foreigner made her the most hated woman in France; the remark attributed to her that the people should eat cake is not documented. During the revolution she pressed the hesitant king to resist and in 1791 promoted the failed flight to Varennes as well as secret contacts with Austria. After the fall of the monarchy she was separated from her children, charged with high treason before the revolutionary tribunal and executed on 16 October 1793.
lafayette#role: General and politician in America and France
lafayette#summary: The hero of two worlds, who as a young nobleman fought for American independence and in France argued for a monarchy with a constitution.
lafayette#text: The 19-year-old marquis sailed to America in 1777 against the will of the court, became General Washington's closest confidant and contributed to the victory at Yorktown. In 1789 he presented the National Assembly with the first draft of the Declaration of the Rights of Man, commanded the Paris National Guard and created the flag of the revolution with the tricolor. As a moderate supporter of a constitutional monarchy he was caught between the fronts: the radicals accused him of protecting the king, and after the fall of the monarchy in 1792 he fled, only to fall into Austrian captivity, from which Napoleon secured his release in 1797. Under Napoleon he withdrew from public life, made a triumphal tour of the United States in 1824 and in 1830 helped Louis-Philippe to the throne, wrapping him in the tricolor on the balcony of the town hall.
klemens-von-metternich#role: Austrian foreign minister and state chancellor
klemens-von-metternich#summary: The architect of the Vienna order, who sought for four decades to secure Europe against revolution, liberalism and nationalism.
klemens-von-metternich#text: Metternich came from a Rhenish noble family that fled to Vienna before the French revolutionary armies, and in Habsburg service rose to become ambassador in Paris and, in 1809, foreign minister. He arranged Napoleon's marriage to the emperor's daughter Marie Louise, brought Austria over to the allies in 1813 and shaped the Congress of Vienna with the aim of a balance among the great powers. After 1815 he organized surveillance of the press, universities and associations through the Carlsbad Decrees, the German Confederation and congresses of the Holy Alliance; for liberals his name became the very emblem of oppression. The March Revolution of 1848 forced the 74-year-old chancellor to flee to England; he returned in 1851 and died in Vienna in 1859.
miguel-hidalgo#role: Priest and leader of the Mexican independence uprising
